job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
I reviewed only the text you pasted, so I haven't checked it against the pre-amendment version or the DSHMRA text. Items are in section order, with cross-cutting issues at the end.

**Most serious:** #21 (the sunset contradicts the indefinite ban), #8-9 (grandfather clause), #24 (conflict with existing law), #1 and #5 (easy to structure around), #13-14 (no real enforcement), and #17 and #23 (date problems).

1. **§2(1)(A), per-vessel threshold.** The 10,000 t/yr test applies to "a single vessel," so an operator can run several vessels, or rotate them, with each staying under the line. Pilot- and demonstration-scale mining stays legal, and the text doesn't say whether the year is calendar or rolling, or whether tonnage is wet or dry weight.

2. **§2(1)(A), "recovery" and "mineral resources."** Neither term is defined. Activity that disturbs the seabed without lifting material to the surface (cutting, crushing, collector testing) may fall outside "recovery," and "other mineral resources" could be argued not to cover crusts, sulfides, or muds. At-sea processing and discharge of tailings are not addressed.

3. **§2(1)(A), depth and geography.** The text doesn't say how or where the 200 m depth is measured, and "deep seabed" is never defined. It's unclear whether the Act reaches the U.S. EEZ and continental shelf, areas beyond national jurisdiction, or foreign waters. Mining at 150 m is excluded despite the title.

4. **§2(1)(B), the Secretary catch-all.** "The Secretary" is never identified (Commerce? Interior? NOAA?), and there is no deadline, procedure, or criteria for what counts as "comparable" risk. Because it depends on a determination, an unsympathetic administration can simply never make one. Tying criminal liability to an undefined future determination also invites vagueness and nondelegation challenges.

5. **§2(2), "U.S. person."** It covers only citizens and "corporations organized under the laws of a State." That arguably excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, D.C. or territorial entities, permanent residents, and foreign subsidiaries or joint ventures controlled by U.S. companies, so restructuring is easy.

6. **§3(a), jurisdictional hook.** "Person" is undefined, and "in the United States" fits poorly with activity at sea. It's unclear whether U.S.-flagged vessels, vessels in U.S. waters, or port calls count, and foreign operators outside the U.S. are not reached. "Engage in" also doesn't clearly cover owning, financing, or contracting.

7. **§3, no ancillary or demand-side prohibitions.** There is no ban on importing, processing, buying, or financing seabed minerals, and no aiding-and-abetting, conspiracy, or port-access provisions. U.S. firms could offtake from foreign operations or fund them.

8. **§3(b), scope of the grandfather clause.** Exploration licenses generally don't authorize commercial recovery, so it's unclear what is protected. Read broadly, it exempts commercial-scale mining with no cap, area limit, or expiration, and it doesn't address renewals, extensions, amendments, or transfers. "Exploration license" and its issuing authority (NOAA, ISA-sponsored, foreign state) are undefined.

9. **§3(b), cutoff date.** Keying the exemption to "before the date of enactment" creates an incentive to obtain or expand licenses before enactment, and an administration favorable to mining could issue them. A cutoff at introduction, or a bar on amendments or expansions, would close this.

10. **§3(c), environmental assessment exemption.** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, "for the purpose of" is subjective, and there is no tonnage cap, permit, independence requirement, or bar on selling recovered material. Large test-mining campaigns could be labeled "assessment."

11. **§4(a), registry coverage.** The registry covers only vessels over 5,000 GT "equipped for recovery," which is undefined. Smaller vessels, vessels retrofitted after registering, and support, shuttle, and processing ships fall outside, and the 5,000 GT line doesn't track the 10,000 t threshold. There is also no registration deadline (before operating?), no required content, and no public access.

12. **§4(b), self-certified reports.** Required data fields (tonnage, location, depth, dates, equipment) aren't specified, and there is no verification, audit, inspection, or vessel-tracking requirement. NOAA would have no reliable way to tell whether the §2 threshold is crossed.

13. **§4 and §5, registry has no enforcement.** §5 penalizes only violations of §3, so failing to register, failing to report, or filing false reports carries no penalty under this Act. Only general false-statement law might apply.

14. **Whole bill, no lead enforcer or implementing authority.** There is no rulemaking authority, designated enforcement agency (NOAA, Coast Guard, DOJ), inspection or boarding power, vessel forfeiture, or port-denial authority. There is also no appropriations authorization, which makes enforcement against foreign-flagged vessels especially hard.

15. **Whole bill, no citizen-suit provision.** If the executive branch declines to enforce, nobody else can step in. A citizen-suit clause would also reduce reliance on agency discretion.

16. **§5(a), civil penalty design.** It is "not more than" $1M/day, with no minimum, no penalty factors, no inflation adjustment, and no disgorgement or forfeiture. It also doesn't say who assesses the penalty or by what procedure, and it grants no injunctive authority. A cap alone may be cheap relative to commercial-scale revenue.

17. **§5(a) vs. §8, conflicting dates.** Penalties apply to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but the Act doesn't take effect until 180 days later. Defendants can argue nothing was unlawful during the gap, and the mismatch invites fair-notice and retroactivity challenges.

18. **§5(b), "willfully."** Prosecutors must prove knowledge that the conduct was unlawful. Combined with the vague definitions and exemptions, defendants can claim a good-faith belief they were under the threshold or within §3(b) or (c). There is no lesser knowing or negligent tier and no corporate-officer liability language.

19. **§6, international agreement.** "Shall seek to negotiate" requires no outcome, reporting to Congress, or consequence, and it's unclear whether "not later than 18 months" modifies the negotiating or the agreement. "Equivalent" is undefined, and there is no tie to the ISA or authority for trade measures. This is a policy statement, not an enforceable duty.

20. **§7(a), lifting standard.** "Serious harm" is undefined and weaker than the "irreversible" harm framing. There is no requirement that the National Academies report be commissioned, funded, independent, or timed, and Congress need not follow it ("acting on"). The burden is effectively on opponents rather than on proponents to show safety.

21. **§7(a) vs. §7(b), internal contradiction.** §7(a) makes the ban indefinite until Congress finds mining safe, while §7(b) ends the Act automatically after 10 years regardless of science. A court would likely give effect to the specific sunset, so the real ban is 10 years, which contradicts our permanent-prohibition goal.

22. **§7(b), no savings clause.** "Cease to have effect" is not clearly a repeal, so it's ambiguous whether penalties for pre-sunset violations can still be pursued. Operators can also plan around the sunset and the §8 gap, holding assets until the ban lapses.

23. **§8, 180-day delay.** Operators can use the gap to ramp up, sign contracts, and build reliance or vested-rights arguments. §3(b) protects only licenses issued before enactment, but nothing stops new recovery activity or permit processing during the gap.

24. **No relationship to existing law.** The bill doesn't amend or repeal the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. 1401 et seq., the NOAA licensing and permitting regime; please verify the cite), and it doesn't bar agencies from processing or issuing new licenses or permits. That leaves two statutes pointing in opposite directions, and agencies could keep processing pending applications. It also doesn't address recent executive actions favoring seabed mineral development.

25. **No findings, authority statement, or severability clause.** Without severability, a court striking one provision (for example §2(1)(B)) could jeopardize the whole Act. Findings and a statement of constitutional authority would also help defend against challenges.

26. **No takings or transition provisions.** Companies with sunk investments, pending applications, or non-grandfathered licenses are likely to bring takings or due process claims. The bill says nothing about compensation, wind-down, or how pending applications are treated.

Before the markup, I'd confirm the legal characterizations (especially #17, #21, #22, #24, and #26) with counsel or Legislative Counsel. I'd also ask the sponsor's staff what the October 6 manager's amendment changed, since the §3(b) and §7(b) language may be new.
